consensus_summary: “Life,” especially “the life,” centrally denotes eternal or divine life received through Christ and may identify Christ himself as its embodiment and source. Covenant obedience and flourishing are recognized as secondary or context-specific meanings.
book_summary: “Life” is covenant existence: the manner of life found by walking in God’s Way according to his law.
consensus_core_identification: Divine or eternal life in Christ, including Christ himself as “the Life.”
book_core_identification: A covenantal mode of existence characterized by obedience to God’s Way and law.
boundary_disagreement: The book elevates Deuteronomic covenant life from a recognized secondary usage to the governing identification and applies it to Christological and Way texts. It thereby reclassifies cases the consensus primarily treats as Christ himself or the saving life he imparts.
material_contradiction: In the same definite or Christological context, Christ/divine life and a law-directed covenant manner of living are different referents. The book’s common-view note confirms that its identification is presented in contrast to, rather than merely as elaboration of, the standard identification.
rationale: The reading is not novel because the consensus explicitly recognizes covenant blessing, obedience, and righteous flourishing as a common alternative. Nevertheless, the book replaces the consensus’s central referent with that alternative rather than preserving and merely narrowing the Christological or eternal-life identification. Some extensions overlap because covenant communion and eternal life can be related, but relation does not make their core identifications equivalent.
strongest_objection: Deuteronomy 30:19–20 and Leviticus 18:5 directly support a covenant-obedience sense of life, so the entry could be viewed as selecting a legitimate contextual strand rather than denying the Christological one. However, John 14:6 identifies Jesus as “the life,” while Matthew 7:14 distinguishes the way from the life to which it leads; the printed citations alone do not establish the book’s equation across these contexts.
